svg.text: A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (any Pi works), the e-ink HAT on the header, a small LCD on eight jumpers, the rest over USB. Physical pin numbers; pin 1 is the corner pin nearest the microSD slot.
Waveshare e-Paper HAT, any of the three
Plugs onto all 40 pins. It uses SPI0 — MOSI 19,
SCLK 23, CE0 24 — and DC 22, RST 11, BUSY 18, PWR
12: the pins marked in red. The 2.7" adds four
its 40-pin socket, straight onto the Pi's header
Instead of the e-ink HAT, the speaker and the
microphone: its 1.69" colour LCD is the screen, with
two mics, a speaker, a button and an LED. It takes
the whole header too, so it's either this or the
e-ink HAT — and no second LCD, the HAT's screen is
The Zero's one micro-USB OTG port, through a hub
with its own power supply (a data/OTG adapter, not a
Webcam, or an OBSBOT that pans and tilts
the live view, the watcher, photos
where it is, for the weather and the map
A Pi camera goes on the CSI ribbon instead (the Zero's
Eight wires to the header; each pad
below has its pin, and the pin its tag.
The HAT covers the header, so fit an extra-tall
stacking header under it, or a 40-pin breakout, and
take the LCD's eight wires from that. The LCD shares
MOSI, SCLK, 3V3 and GND with the e-ink and has its
own chip-select (CE1), so neither waits on the
other. Don't copy Waveshare's example pins (DC 22,
CE0, BL 18): those are the HAT's.
Long or untidy jumpers: drop the SPI clock to 16 MHz in Settings.
A UPS HAT sits under the Pi and feeds the header's 5
V pins, so a power cut doesn't take the screen down;
without one, the Pi's own PWR port is fine.
Everything else is powered from the Pi (the HAT, the
LCD at 3.3 V) or from the hub's own supply (the USB
